title: Record companies ignore the band's instrumentals; critics who scorned bebop
summary: The band cut only Opus X and Second Balcony Jump as instrumentals; companies thought only Billy sold records and critics later praised what they once panned.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: The other thing about the band was that by these greedy record companies... Whenever there was a record date made, throughout the whole extent of the band (which the band lasted a little over two years, I think), the band recorded really only two instrumentals. One of them was this "Opus X" of mine and the other was a thing that Jerry Valentine wrote called "Second Balcony Jump," which he had written before for Earl Hines. But other than those two instrumentals, the band never recorded any of the instrumentals. And I thought it was a shame.

But these record companies were so hung up on thinking that Billy was the sole record-seller, that they didn't understand the instrumentals any more than some of the other people in New York who thought that the band stunk and didn't understand what was happening, that this Bebop and all of that was nothing. There are guys that are writing in the Downbeat and critics, some critics now that are here writing and making all sorts of nice things and talkin' all knowledgeable about Bebop, who were some of the same ones that was puttin' it down when it was in its infancy. I've even read a couple of books by guys who proved to be so knowledgeable about everything, including being close friends to Charlie Parker and Dizzy and all that, who at that particular time was doing everything they could do to hurt them. But that's I guess the story of a lot of things that happen when it's new -- people just don't understand.
Nevertheless, these record companies missed out on so much by not recording these instrumental things that the band was playing.
